summary:
ASTROLENZA is a visor-first crew-health and spacesuit monitoring prototype designed to help astronauts and mission teams recognise emerging health and equipment problems earlier.

The platform visualises simulated crew and suit telemetry, including heart rate, respiration, blood oxygen saturation, oxygen and carbon dioxide partial pressures, internal suit pressure, gas flow, pump speed, temperature, battery status and movement. Its probabilistic reasoning engine estimates sensor states, ranks potential faults, examines supporting evidence and recommends the next most useful measurement. It also provides a conditional time-to-hazard projection, helping users understand how a developing fault could progress if left unattended.

ASTROLENZA transforms monitoring into an interactive decision-support experience. Its visor notifications allow a crew member to attend to, escalate, resolve or close an alert while preserving the underlying fault state. The project demonstrates how explainable, human-supervised intelligence could support safer and more autonomous human spaceflight. The current prototype uses synthetic telemetry and public NASA reference resources; it is not a live NASA data system or certified flight platform.
details:
What ASTROLENZA does

ASTROLENZA is an intelligent crew-health and spacesuit monitoring prototype built around an immersive, visor-first interface. Rather than presenting astronauts and mission operators with a conventional dashboard, it places the astronaut and surrounding mission environment at the centre of the experience, with spatial suit indicators, contextual telemetry and interactive mission alerts.

The platform brings together three main perspectives:

  • Mission: A situational overview of the crew member, suit condition, mission environment and emerging alerts.
  • Suit: A detailed view of individual suit regions and their associated sensor readings, estimated condition and fault evidence.
  • Intelligence: A decision-support view that presents fault hypotheses, supporting evidence, projected hazards and recommended follow-up measurements.

Health and suit monitoring

The current visor models 13 telemetry channels, including:

  • Internal suit pressure.
  • Oxygen partial pressure and carbon dioxide partial pressure.
  • Gas flow and cooling-pump RPM.
  • Skin and outlet temperature.
  • Heart rate, respiration and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂).
  • Battery status, inertial measurement and radiation context.

Core temperature is inferred by the model rather than received as a direct sensor reading.

Blood pressure is part of the broader longitudinal crew-health concept, but it is not currently a direct live telemetry channel in the submitted v18 visor. It should therefore be treated as an extension of the health-monitoring model, not a currently measured input.

Fault identification and failure classification

ASTROLENZA analyses sensor behaviour and equipment relationships to identify possible developing faults. Its supported demonstration fault set includes cooling-pump degradation, suit leakage, scrubber degradation, high metabolic load, skin-sensor bias, flow-sensor bias and fan failure.

The system is designed to distinguish a failing physical subsystem from a faulty sensor. This matters because an unreliable sensor should not automatically be interpreted as a real equipment failure.

When a fault is identified, the reasoning model ranks possible explanations, evaluates supporting evidence and identifies the next most useful measurement.

Time-to-hazard analysis

A central feature is conditional time-to-hazard projection. Instead of only reporting that a parameter is outside its expected range, the model estimates how a developing condition could progress towards a defined threshold under the current simulated scenario.

This provides a time-sensitive view of potential failure progression. It is a conditional projection within a 30-minute horizon, not a guaranteed countdown or prediction of an actual disaster.

Mission communications and human response

The Mission visor can produce simulated plain-text notifications. Each notification can be attended to, escalated, resolved, closed or terminated.

Attending an alert takes the user directly to the affected crew member and relevant suit region. Escalation increases the alert priority. Resolution runs the mapped simulated recovery action. Closing or terminating a message does not silently erase the underlying simulated fault.

This keeps the crew member or operator involved in the decision rather than allowing an automated system to silently make operational decisions.

How AI and data analysis are used

ASTROLENZA uses a probabilistic intelligence and decision-support approach. Its analytical foundations include Kalman-style sensor-state estimation, Bayesian fault-hypothesis ranking, evidence and residual analysis, hazard projection and value-of-information reasoning.

These techniques help the system estimate what may be happening, determine which explanation is best supported by the available measurements, and identify which additional observation would be most useful.

The system's runtime reasoning is not a conversational chatbot or a generative AI diagnosis service. It is an algorithmic model operating on the prototype's simulated telemetry and defined scenarios. No real astronaut medical records or live NASA crew telemetry are being processed.

Data sources and NASA resources

The project references NASA human-spaceflight standards, crew-health research, standard measurement frameworks and space-weather resources. These references inform the intended measurement domains, safety context and evidence structure.

NASA resources include NASA-STD-3001, NASA Standard Measures, NASA's Crew Health and Performance Integrated Data Architecture research, the Human Research Roadmap, the Human Research Program and DONKI.

Other research references include published work on sleep restriction and cognitive performance, the effects of carbon dioxide exposure on decision-making, and longitudinal medical monitoring during long-duration spaceflight.

The project distinguishes public reference material from simulated telemetry. The current v18 visor does not connect to live NASA data feeds. NASA OSDR, Life Sciences Data Archive and RadLab interfaces were specified in an earlier project model as potential research-data connectors, but those adapters are stubbed rather than actively retrieving datasets.

Technology and development

The prototype is implemented as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with React 18 and ReactDOM 18 for the interface. It uses embedded visual assets, responsive layouts, suit-region indicators, interactive navigation and simulated telemetry scenarios.

The development process focused on preserving the underlying estimation and fault-reasoning model while creating a more intuitive visor-first experience. Browser-based interface smoke tests covered mission navigation, suit inspection, intelligence rendering, alert handling and a mobile viewport.

Creativity, benefits and intended impact

ASTROLENZA combines crew-health awareness, environmental and suit monitoring, fault identification and decision support in one spatial interface. Its originality lies in connecting sensor-level information to an understandable human response workflow.

The intended benefit is to help crews and mission-support teams move from passive monitoring towards earlier investigation, better fault discrimination and more informed action. The approach could contribute to greater crew autonomy and more effective monitoring during long-duration missions.

ASTROLENZA is a research and demonstration prototype. Its telemetry is synthetic, its time-to-hazard estimates are conditional, and it has not been medically validated, certified by NASA or approved for flight operations.
